quote: the truth about the present life
note: Beatrice's attack on human greed and misrule, which closed Canto 27.

quote: a candle's flame reflected in a mirror
note: Dante first sees the light of God as a reflection in Beatrice's eyes, then turns around to look at the thing itself, and finds it exactly as her eyes showed it.
The language of love poetry, kept even here: her eyes were the trap in which Love caught him, long ago in Florence.

context: Dante entered it in Canto 27. It holds no star or planet. What he sees here instead is a vision of God and the angels.

note: God, shown as a point: something with no size and no parts, which cannot be divided or measured. It is the smallest thing Dante has ever seen and the brightest.
The ring of light that appears around the sun or moon when it shines through thin mist.

context: The first of nine rings of fire circling the point. Each is one order of angels. The nearest to God is the smallest, fastest and brightest.

quote: whatever motion fastest girds our world
note: The Primum Mobile itself, the fastest thing in the physical universe. The innermost ring of angels spins faster still.
Iris, goddess of the rainbow, who carried messages for Juno, queen of the gods. Even a rainbow completed into a full circle would be too small to hold the seventh ring.
A near quotation from Aristotle's Metaphysics, where he says of the first mover: on such a principle depend the heavens and nature.

quote: the blazing love that spurs it on
note: What moves the angels is love. The nearer a ring is to God, the more it loves, and the faster it turns.

Dante's difficulty. In the physical universe the smallest sphere, the Moon's, is the slowest and lowest, and the spheres grow swifter and holier as they grow wider. Here it is the other way round: the smallest ring is the swiftest and nearest God.
The visible universe: the earth at the center with the nine heavens around it.
The rings of angels are the pattern, and the heavens are the copy made from it. Dante expects a copy to look like its pattern.

Beatrice's answer. In bodies, size shows power: the bigger the sphere, the more good it holds and pours down. Among the angels, power shows as nearness to God. So the two orders match by power, not by size.
The Primum Mobile, the largest heaven, which carries all the others round with it.

quote: the circle that most loves and knows
note: The Seraphim, the smallest ring and the highest order. They turn the largest heaven.

Each heaven is turned by one order of angels, called Intelligences by the philosophers. Going up: the Moon by the Angels, Mercury by the Archangels, Venus by the Principalities, the Sun by the Powers, Mars by the Virtues, Jupiter by the Dominions, Saturn by the Thrones, the fixed stars by the Cherubim, the Primum Mobile by the Seraphim.

Boreas in the Italian, the north wind of the Greeks and Romans. Winds were pictured as faces blowing with puffed cheeks. From his milder cheek comes the wind that sweeps the clouds away and leaves the sky clear.
The rings throw off sparks, and each spark is an angel. Dante used the same picture of glowing iron for the sun's brightness in Paradiso 1.

An old story. The inventor of chess asked his king for one grain of wheat on the first square of the board, two on the second, four on the third, doubling each time to the sixty-fourth. The total is more than eighteen million million million grains. The angels outnumber even that.
A Hebrew cry of praise, shouted by the crowds when Christ rode into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:9).
Dante uses the Latin word "ubi", "where", a term of the philosophy schools for a thing's place. The angels have kept the place God gave them since their creation, and always will.

The highest order. In Isaiah 6 they are six-winged beings who stand above God's throne crying "Holy, holy, holy". Their name was understood to mean "burning", and they stand for the most ardent love of God.
The second order. In the Bible cherubim guard the gate of Eden and God's throne. Theologians associated them with fullness of knowledge.
The bonds of love that tie each ring to the point and keep it circling.
The third order. God's judgments were said to rest on them and be handed down through them. In Paradiso 9 a soul calls them mirrors from which God's judgment shines.
The nine orders are grouped in three sets of three, called hierarchies. The number mirrors the Trinity.

Beatrice settles a debate of the medieval schools: does the joy of Heaven lie first in knowing God or in loving him? She answers with Thomas Aquinas that seeing comes first, and love follows from it. Franciscan thinkers tended to put love first.
How much each angel or soul sees depends on merit, and merit comes from two things together: God's grace, freely given, and the will that accepts it.
Dante's Italian says "nightly Aries". The constellation of the Ram is in the night sky in autumn, when the leaves fall. No autumn ever comes to this spring.
Three orders, each singing its own part of one song.

The names of the middle orders come from Saint Paul's letters, which list "thrones, dominions, principalities, powers" among the things God created (Colossians 1:16; also Ephesians 1:21). Later theologians took the lists as ranks of angels.
"Virtue" here means strength or power to act, not moral goodness.
The order of the angels sent with the greatest messages. The Bible names Michael, Gabriel, who announced Christ's birth to Mary, and Raphael.
The lowest order and the nearest to humankind. The word means "messengers" in Greek, and it also serves as the common name for all nine orders.

quote: all draw toward God and all attract
note: A chain of love. Every order looks up to God and is drawn by him, and in turn draws the order below it upward. Through the heavens they turn, the same pull reaches the earth.

context: The order of the nine ranks that Beatrice has just given is his, from The Celestial Hierarchy. Dante had ranked them differently in his earlier Convivio, so he too is corrected here.

Gregory arranged the orders differently: in one of his lists the Principalities and the Virtues change places. On reaching Heaven he saw that he had been wrong, and smiled at it. A mistake about angels is no cause for grief among the blessed.

quote: the one who saw it here
context: Paul wrote that he was once caught up to Heaven and heard things that may not be told (2 Corinthians 12). Dionysius was believed to be his convert, and so to have learned about the angels from an eyewitness.
